title: Managing Dependencies Without Finding Someone to Blame
summary: Late dependencies turn into blame. Write each one down, make "owner" mean the next action, plan handoffs with slack and design the fallback before you need it.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Two days before release, someone posts in the channel: "We're blocked on the payments API." It sounds sudden. It isn't. The API contract had been "almost final" for two weeks. QA had been waiting on test data from another team since the sprint started. One empty state still had no design. Everyone was busy and nobody was slacking. The dependency map just lived in five different heads, so the delay only became visible when it hit the date.

Dependencies aren't proof that someone did a bad job. Software is connected by nature: the frontend waits on an API, a release waits on legal wording, a migration has to fit the support team's calendar. They do cost something, though. Team Topologies puts it bluntly: "Nothing kills productivity faster than one team waiting on another team" (Team Topologies key concepts). So the first move is to have fewer of them. The second is to make the ones you keep visible early, and to talk about them in a way that doesn't make people hide them.

Why late dependencies turn into blame

When a dependency shows up late, everyone reaches for the same script. The waiting team feels blocked. The providing team feels attacked. A manager asks whose delay this is. Nobody in that room is a bad person. The setup simply hid the risk until the schedule had no slack left, and blame filled the gap.

The sociologist Ron Westrum sorted organizations by how they handle information, and DORA's research summary lays out his table (Generative organizational culture). In what he calls pathological cultures, "messengers punished," "bridging discouraged" and "failure leads to scapegoating." In generative cultures, "messengers trained," "bridging encouraged," "risks are shared" and "failure leads to inquiry." DORA's research links the generative kind to better software delivery and organizational performance.

That table explains why dependencies go dark. If saying "we'll be late on the API" gets you a grilling, people wait until they're sure, which means they wait until it's too late. Google's SRE book makes the same point about incidents: blameless postmortems focus on contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team," because otherwise "people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment" (Postmortem Culture). A dependency slip is a small incident that hasn't happened yet. The person who flags it early deserves a thank-you.

Write the dependency down

A useful dependency note has six fields, and it fits in one message:

  • What's needed, specific enough to check ("payment status endpoint with the refund field," not "the API").
  • Who owns the next action.
  • The need-by date, meaning when you need it, which isn't the same as their estimate.
  • Any decision still pending, and who makes it.
  • The fallback if it slips.
  • The early signal that means the plan is at risk.
Example note

Need: payment status endpoint with the refund field, on staging. Next action: Lan (payments) to confirm the field name by Wednesday. Need-by: Monday the 14th so QA has three days. Pending: whether partial refunds are in scope (PO decides Tuesday). Fallback: frontend uses a fixture behind the flag. Risk signal: contract not frozen by Wednesday.

Nothing heavy there. It just pulls what's scattered across private DMs and half-remembered meetings into one place the whole team can read.

"Owner" means next action, not culprit

The owner field matters, and it can turn into a weapon if you let it. Owning a dependency means someone keeps the next step visible and moving. It doesn't mean that person takes the hit when reality changes. Accountability asks "what has to happen next, and who can move it?" Blame asks "who made us uncomfortable?" The first question gets you to release day. The second gets you a team that pads every estimate and announces nothing until it's certain.

Plan the handoff with some slack

Mike Cohn's Agile Estimating and Planning has a chapter on multi-team projects (Chapter 18, "Planning the Multiple-Team Project") with advice that holds up well (book page). His baseline is a rolling lookahead plan covering the next two or three iterations, so both teams can see the handoff coming. He prefers handoffs that land between iterations, because committing to work that depends on something "due in a few days" is shaky. When dependencies get too tangled for that, his first recourse is to reduce them. If you can't, add a feeding buffer to the iterations that deliver what another team needs. His one-line version: "if your team needs something from my team tomorrow at 8:00 A.M., my team shouldn't plan on finishing it at 7:59."

The same idea shows up in release planning as a visible buffer (more in Agile release planning). And when the thing you hand over still has open questions, say so in the handoff itself (making handoffs honest about what's unknown).

Design the fallback before you need it

A fallback is one of the kindest things you can plan. API late? The frontend builds against a fixture behind a feature flag. Final copy not ready? QA tests the behavior with placeholder text. Partner integration slipping? Release to a smaller segment first. A fallback doesn't remove the dependency. It takes away the pressure that turns a normal delay into a crisis, and with it most of the urge to find someone to blame.

Give dependencies a rhythm

A weekly status meeting is usually too slow for a dependency that's moving. A short async update works better: current state, next action, risk, help needed. If nothing changed, post that too: "No change, still on track for Wednesday." When people hear nothing, they fill the gap with their own story, and under pressure those stories are rarely generous.

The best dependency board is the one the team actually checks before decisions harden, pretty or not. It lets product trim scope while trimming is cheap, QA plan coverage, engineering split work differently, and leads see the risk without asking for a heroic explanation at the end.

Try this week

  • List every "we're waiting on..." in your current sprint and write each one as a six-field note.
  • For each, ask whether you could remove the dependency instead of managing it.
  • Pick the riskiest one and write its fallback today.
  • Next time someone flags a slip early, thank them in the channel where everyone can see it.

Managing dependencies without blame still means having the hard conversation. You just have it while there's time to choose. Seen early, a blocker is a planning problem. Seen two days before release, it turns into a trial. Pick the planning problem.

faqs.q: Why do dependency delays so often turn into blame?
faqs.a: Because they surface late, when the schedule has no slack left. The waiting team feels blocked, the providing team feels attacked and someone asks whose fault it is. Ron Westrum's research, summarized by DORA, shows the pattern: in cultures where messengers get punished, people hide bad news until it's too late.

faqs.q: What should a dependency note include?
faqs.a: Six things: what's needed (specific enough to check), who owns the next action, the date you need it by, any pending decision and who makes it, the fallback if it slips, and the early signal that the plan is at risk. One short message is enough.

faqs.q: How should teams plan a handoff between them?
faqs.a: Mike Cohn's Agile Estimating and Planning starts with a rolling lookahead plan over the next two or three iterations and handoffs that land between iterations. If the dependencies are too tangled for that, try to reduce them, and when you can't, add a feeding buffer: if your team needs something at 8:00 A.M. tomorrow, mine shouldn't plan to finish at 7:59.

faqs.q: What's the difference between accountability and blame?
faqs.a: Accountability asks what has to happen next and who can move it. Blame asks who made everyone uncomfortable. Owning a dependency means keeping the next step visible and moving, not taking the hit when plans change.
